title: Power and energy potential study
summary: P = 9.81 Q H eta is the one equation everything rests on, and the trap is using GROSS head where NET head belongs. The flow duration curve is the central diagram: the installed capacity is read from a high-flow exceedance while the firm power that earns the better tariff comes from the low-flow end. Learn the load factor family carefully, because capacity factor, load factor, utilisation factor and diversity factor are defined with different denominators and are routinely confused.

sections.heading: Power, head and energy
sections.body:
**The fundamental equation:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η** watts, or in practical units
> **P (kW) = 9.81 × Q × H × η**  with **Q** in m³/s and **H** in metres

**Overall efficiency η** is the product of the component efficiencies:

> **η = η_turbine × η_generator × η_transformer × η_transmission (to the metering point)**

| Component | Typical efficiency |
|---|---|
| **Turbine** | 0.85 – 0.93 |
| **Generator** | 0.95 – 0.98 |
| Transformer | 0.98 – 0.99 |
| **Overall (plant)** | **0.80 – 0.90** |

A quick field estimate used in reconnaissance: **P (kW) ≈ 8 × Q × H**, taking η ≈ 0.82.

**Gross and net head — the standard trap:**

| Head | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Gross head H_g** | The **difference in water level** between the intake (or forebay) and the tailrace |
| **Net (effective) head H_n** | **Gross head MINUS all hydraulic losses** in the waterway |

> **POWER MUST BE COMPUTED ON THE NET HEAD.** Using gross head overstates the output — a frequent and consequential error.

**Where the losses occur:**

| Loss | Typical magnitude |
|---|---|
| Intake and trashrack | Small; rises sharply as the rack clogs |
| **Settling basin** | Small |
| **Headrace (canal or tunnel) friction** | Can be substantial over a long conveyance |
| Forebay entry, bends | Minor losses |
| **Penstock friction and bends** | Usually held to **3 – 5% of gross head** |
| Valve | Minor |
| **Total** | Commonly **5 – 10% of gross head** |

The **penstock loss allowance of 3–5%** is itself a design decision, not a given: a larger penstock loses less head but costs more steel, which is the economic diameter problem treated in a later subchapter.

**Energy:**

> **E (kWh) = P (kW) × t (hours)**
> **Annual energy = Σ (P at each flow × duration at that flow)** over the year

So the annual energy is computed by **stepping through the flow duration curve**, and the calculation is a summation rather than a single multiplication — which is exactly why the flow duration curve is the central diagram of the subchapter.

**A worked illustration.** A scheme with gross head 120 m, losses 8%, design flow 4 m³/s and overall efficiency 0.85:

> Net head = 120 × 0.92 = **110.4 m**
> P = 9.81 × 4 × 110.4 × 0.85 = **3,682 kW ≈ 3.7 MW**

Had gross head been used: 9.81 × 4 × 120 × 0.85 = 4,002 kW — an **overstatement of 8.7%**, which on a marginal project is the difference between viability and not.

sections.heading: The flow duration curve and firm power
sections.body:
**The flow duration curve (FDC)** plots **discharge against the percentage of time it is equalled or exceeded**. It is constructed by ranking the whole flow record in descending order and computing each value's exceedance probability.

**Reading it:**

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Q₄₀** | The flow **exceeded 40% of the time** |
| **Q₉₅** | Exceeded 95% of the time — a near-minimum flow |
| Q₁₀ | Exceeded only 10% of the time — a high flow |

Note the direction: a **higher subscript means a LOWER flow**, because a smaller flow is exceeded more often.

**What the shape tells you:**

| Shape | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **FLAT** curve | **Well-regulated** flow — a large groundwater or snowmelt contribution, or an upstream reservoir. Good for hydropower: reliable output |
| **STEEP** curve | A **flashy** river — high monsoon peaks, very low dry-season flow. Needs **storage** to be useful |

Most Nepali rivers give **steep** curves, which is the quantitative statement of the monsoon problem: the plant can use only a fraction of the monsoon flow (limited by its installed capacity) and is starved in the dry season.

**Its two uses, at opposite ends of the curve** — and this is the substance of the subchapter:

| Purpose | Read at | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Installed capacity** (design flow) | **Q₄₀** conventionally | A high-flow exceedance, so the plant is large enough to use the abundant season |
| **FIRM (primary) power** | **Q₉₅ to Q₁₀₀** | The flow available **almost all the time**, hence the power that can be **guaranteed** |

**Firm and secondary power:**

| Term | Definition | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Firm (primary, dependable) power** | Power available **95–100% of the time** — guaranteed | **Higher tariff** — the grid can rely on it |
| **Secondary power** | The surplus available only **seasonally** | Lower tariff — the buyer cannot depend on it |

**Firm power commands the higher price** because a power system must meet its load at every instant. Energy that is available only in the monsoon has value, but it cannot displace the capacity the system must build for the dry season — so it is worth less per unit. That is the economic reason Nepali PPAs distinguish **wet and dry season rates**, with dry-season energy paid substantially more.

**It also explains the appeal of storage.** A reservoir **converts secondary power into firm power** by moving monsoon water into the dry season. That conversion is the whole economic case for a storage project, and it is why such projects are strategically valuable even when their cost per kWh looks unfavourable against a run-of-river scheme.

**The design flow optimisation.** Selecting the design flow is the central economic decision, and the trade-off is direct:

| Higher design flow | Lower design flow |
|---|---|
| **Larger plant, higher capacity** | Smaller, cheaper plant |
| More energy in the monsoon | Monsoon surplus **spilled unused** |
| **Lower plant (capacity) factor** — the plant stands partly idle much of the year | **Higher plant factor** — operates near capacity most of the time |
| Higher capital cost per kWh generated | Lower |

The optimum is found by computing the **annual energy and the capital cost for a range of design flows** and selecting the one giving the **lowest levelised cost of energy** or the highest net present value. **Q₄₀ is a conventional starting point in Nepali practice, not a rule** — the right value depends on the shape of the FDC, the tariff structure (particularly the wet/dry differential) and the cost function of the particular site.

**Constructing the FDC where there is no gauge** — the usual Nepali situation. The record is **transferred** from a gauged catchment:

> **Q_site = Q_gauged × (A_site/A_gauged)^n**, with a correction for the difference in **rainfall and elevation**

with n often taken near 1 for similar catchments. Regional methods (the **WECS/DHM regional method** for Nepal) estimate flows from catchment area, the area below 5000 m elevation, and monsoon rainfall. The uncertainty is significant and **propagates directly into the energy estimate**, so it should be stated rather than concealed — and a **gauge installed at the site early** is worth more than any amount of transfer refinement.

sections.heading: The load factor family
sections.body:
These four are defined with **different denominators** and are routinely confused. The distinction is worth setting out in full, because questions test precisely that.

| Factor | Definition | Denominator |
|---|---|---|
| **Load factor** | **average load / PEAK load** | The **peak load** actually experienced |
| **Capacity (plant) factor** | **average load / INSTALLED capacity** | The plant's **rated capacity** |
| **Utilisation factor** | **peak load / INSTALLED capacity** | The plant's rated capacity |
| **Plant use factor** | energy generated / (capacity × hours actually operated) | Capacity × operating hours |
| **Demand factor** | maximum demand / total connected load | Total connected load |
| **Diversity factor** | **Σ individual maximum demands / system maximum demand** | The **system** maximum |

**The relation among the first three:**

> **Capacity factor = Load factor × Utilisation factor**

which is easily verified: (average/peak) × (peak/installed) = average/installed.

**Interpretation:**

| Factor | High value means |
|---|---|
| **Load factor** | The load is **steady** — a flat demand curve, efficient use of plant |
| **Capacity factor** | The plant is **well utilised** relative to its size |
| **Utilisation factor** | The plant's capacity is nearly fully called upon at the peak |
| **Diversity factor** | Consumers' peaks occur at **different times**, so the system peak is much less than the sum of individual peaks |

**Diversity factor is always ≥ 1**, and the higher it is the better for the utility — because it means less capacity must be built than the sum of consumers' individual maxima would suggest. Its existence is why a distribution transformer serving 50 houses need not be sized for 50 times one house's maximum demand.

**Typical capacity factors:**

| Plant | Capacity factor |
|---|---|
| **Nepali run-of-river hydro** | **0.50 – 0.65** |
| Storage hydro (peaking) | 0.30 – 0.50 (deliberately low — it exists for capacity, not energy) |
| Base-load thermal | 0.70 – 0.90 |
| Solar PV | 0.15 – 0.25 |

**A low capacity factor is not necessarily bad**, and this is worth understanding: a **peaking plant** is built to be available at the daily peak, and it is expected to run only a few hours a day. Its value is in **capacity**, not energy, so judging it by capacity factor misses its purpose. Conversely a run-of-river plant's value is almost entirely **energy**, so its capacity factor matters directly.

**Load curves and load duration curves:**

| Diagram | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Load curve** | Demand against **time of day** — reveals the morning and evening peaks |
| **Load duration curve** | Demand against the **percentage of time** it is exceeded — the demand-side analogue of the FDC |

The **load duration curve** is what determines the **mix of plant** a system needs: the flat base of the curve is met by **base-load** plant (cheap energy, expensive to start and stop), the peak by **peaking** plant (expensive energy, quick to start). Matching plant type to the part of the curve it serves is the basis of generation planning.

**Nepal's load curve** has a pronounced **evening peak** (lighting and cooking, roughly 6–9 pm) and a secondary morning peak, with a deep overnight trough. That shape is why **peaking capacity** is what the system most lacks, and why **PROR schemes** — which can concentrate their generation into the peak hours using a few hours of pondage — are more valuable per MW than pure run-of-river.

**Tariff structures:**

| Tariff | Character |
|---|---|
| **Flat rate** | A fixed charge regardless of consumption; simple, no meter needed; no incentive to economise |
| **Simple (uniform) energy rate** | A single rate per kWh |
| **Block rate** | Rate changes in consumption blocks; can be **progressive** (social) or regressive |
| **Two-part tariff** | A **fixed charge on maximum demand PLUS a running charge on energy** |
| Three-part tariff | Adds a fixed customer charge |
| **Time-of-day (ToD) tariff** | Higher rates at **peak hours** |
| Power factor penalty/incentive | Charges for poor power factor |

**The two-part tariff reflects the utility's actual cost structure**, and that is its justification:

> **Capacity costs are FIXED** — the utility must build plant, lines and transformers sized for the customer's **maximum demand**, whether or not that capacity is used most of the time.
> **Energy costs are VARIABLE** — fuel, or water passed through the turbine.

So charging only for energy makes **peaky consumers under-pay**: a customer who draws a large load for one hour a day forces the utility to build the same capacity as one drawing it continuously, but pays a twenty-fourth as much. The **maximum demand charge** corrects that.

**Time-of-day tariffs** extend the same logic to timing, charging more at the system peak — which both recovers the cost of peaking capacity from those who cause it and gives consumers an incentive to shift load off the peak. Nepal has introduced ToD tariffs for industrial consumers for exactly that reason.

sections.heading: Reservoir capacity, storage and project economics
sections.body:
**The mass curve (Rippl) method** determines the **storage required** to meet a given demand from a variable inflow:

1. Plot the **cumulative inflow** against time over the critical period.
2. Draw **tangents of the demand slope** at each peak of the mass curve.
3. The **maximum vertical intercept** between a tangent and the curve below it is the **required storage**.
4. The period over which that maximum intercept develops is the **critical drought period** — the real design case.

**The critical period is the design case**, not the average year: a reservoir sized for an average year fails in a dry one, which is precisely when it is needed. So the analysis is run on the **driest sequence in the record** — and where the record is short, that sequence may not include the worst drought the site will experience, which is a genuine and unavoidable uncertainty.

**Reservoir storage zones**, from the bottom up:

| Zone | Between | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Dead storage** | The bed and the **minimum drawdown level** | Below the lowest outlet; where **sediment accumulates** |
| **Live (useful) storage** | Minimum drawdown level and **full reservoir level** | **What actually regulates the flow** |
| **Flood control storage** | Conservation level and the flood level | Held empty in the flood season to absorb a flood |
| **Surcharge storage** | Full reservoir level and **maximum water level** | Temporary, during a flood passing the spillway |
| Bank storage | In the banks | Incidental |
| Valley storage | The natural channel volume | Existed before the dam |

**Dead storage sets the reservoir's useful life**, and in the Himalaya this is the binding constraint:

> **Reservoir life = useful (dead) storage capacity / (annual sediment inflow × trap efficiency)**

**Trap efficiency** is the proportion of the inflowing sediment that the reservoir retains. It **rises with the capacity/inflow ratio** — a large reservoir on a small river traps nearly all the sediment (Brune's curves give it), a small pondage traps little.

**Sedimentation is the principal threat to storage projects in Nepal**, and the reason is the sediment load: Himalayan rivers carry among the highest specific sediment yields in the world, from young, steep, tectonically active and increasingly deforested catchments. A reservoir designed for a 100-year life on an underestimated sediment load may lose its live storage in a few decades.

**Mitigation:**

| Measure | Character |
|---|---|
| **Catchment treatment** (afforestation, check dams, terracing) | Addresses the **source**; slow but permanent |
| **Sluicing** | Passing sediment-laden flood flows **through** low-level outlets rather than trapping them |
| **Flushing** | Drawing the reservoir down and scouring deposited sediment out |
| **Density current venting** | Releasing the sediment-laden underflow through a low outlet |
| Dredging | Expensive; a last resort |
| **Providing generous dead storage** | Accepts the sedimentation and designs for it |

**Sluicing and flushing require the outlets and the operating flexibility to be designed in from the start** — a dam without adequate low-level outlets cannot be flushed however much the operator wishes to, which is a design decision with hundred-year consequences.

**Reservoir area–capacity curves** are derived from the **contour map** of the reservoir site: the **area enclosed by each contour** is planimetered, and the volume between successive contours computed by the **trapezoidal**, **prismoidal** or **cone** formula:

> **Cone formula: V = (h/3)(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂))**

The cone formula is more accurate than the trapezoidal where the two areas differ greatly, as they do near the dam where the valley narrows sharply.

**Project economics.**

> **Levelised cost of energy (LCOE) = present value of all costs / present value of all energy produced**

It is the honest basis for comparing projects with different balances of capital and operating cost and different lifetimes.

**Hydropower's economic character** is distinctive and worth stating:

| Feature | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Very high capital cost** | Financing terms dominate the economics |
| **Very low running cost** (no fuel) | Once built, the energy is nearly free |
| **Long life** (50–100 years) | Benefits accrue far into the future |
| **Long construction period** | Interest during construction is a large cost item |

**Therefore the LCOE is extremely sensitive to the DISCOUNT RATE**, and this is the most important economic point about hydropower: because almost all the cost is incurred at the start and almost all the benefit arrives over decades, a **high discount rate makes hydropower look expensive** and a low one makes it look cheap. A thermal plant, whose cost is mostly fuel spread over its life, is far less sensitive.

The practical consequence is that **financing terms matter as much as engineering**. A project at 6% interest over 20 years and the same project at 12% over 10 years have quite different LCOEs, from identical engineering — which is why concessional finance and long tenors are decisive for hydropower in a developing economy, and why the discount rate assumed in an appraisal should always be stated and tested for sensitivity.

**Appraisal criteria**, as applied:

| Criterion | Test |
|---|---|
| **NPV** | Positive at the discount rate |
| **IRR / FIRR** | Exceeds the cost of capital or MARR |
| **EIRR** | For the **economic** appraisal, on shadow prices, including externalities |
| **B/C ratio** | ≥ 1 |
| Payback period | Indicative only; ignores everything after payback |
| **Sensitivity analysis** | On cost overrun, delay, tariff, hydrology, and the **discount rate** |

**Sensitivity analysis is not optional for a hydropower project**, because the two largest uncertainties — **construction cost (chiefly geological) and hydrology** — are both substantial and both capable of moving the result across the viability threshold. An appraisal presenting a single IRR without testing it against a 20% cost overrun and a 10% hydrology shortfall has not been completed.

formulas.label: Power output
formulas.expression: P (kW) = 9.81 × Q × H_net × η     (Q in m³/s, H in m)
formulas.note: Use the NET head. η = turbine × generator × transformer, typically 0.80–0.90. Field estimate P ≈ 8QH.

formulas.label: Net head
formulas.expression: H_net = H_gross − all hydraulic losses     (losses typically 5–10% of gross)
formulas.note: Penstock loss is conventionally held to 3–5% of gross head — itself an economic diameter decision.

formulas.label: Annual energy
formulas.expression: E = Σ (P at each flow × duration at that flow), stepping through the flow duration curve
formulas.note: A summation, not a single multiplication — which is why the FDC is the central diagram.

formulas.label: Flow duration curve — the two readings
formulas.expression: Installed capacity from about Q₄₀ ;   FIRM power from Q₉₅ to Q₁₀₀
formulas.note: A higher subscript means a LOWER flow. Firm power earns the higher tariff; storage converts secondary to firm.

formulas.label: The load factor family
formulas.expression: load factor = avg/PEAK ; capacity factor = avg/INSTALLED ; utilisation = peak/INSTALLED ; diversity = Σ individual maxima / system maximum
formulas.note: Capacity factor = load factor × utilisation factor. Diversity factor is always ≥ 1.

formulas.label: Reservoir life
formulas.expression: life = dead storage capacity / (annual sediment inflow × trap efficiency)
formulas.note: Trap efficiency rises with the capacity/inflow ratio (Brune's curves). The binding constraint in the Himalaya.

formulas.label: Reservoir volume between contours (cone formula)
formulas.note: More accurate than the trapezoidal rule where the areas differ greatly, as they do near the dam.

formulas.label: Levelised cost of energy
formulas.expression: LCOE = PV(all costs) / PV(all energy produced)
formulas.note: Extremely sensitive to the DISCOUNT RATE for hydropower, because cost is front-loaded and benefit is spread.

formulas.label: Flow transfer to an ungauged site
formulas.expression: Q_site = Q_gauged × (A_site/A_gauged)^n, with a rainfall and elevation correction
formulas.note: The uncertainty propagates directly into the energy estimate — state it rather than conceal it.
